analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover emergency room care without prior approval, no matter which hospital a patient reaches.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan emergency-care bill with 242 cosponsors — 81 Republicans and 160 Democrats — never advanced past committee and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: In the mid-1990s many managed-care plans only paid for emergency room visits at hospitals in their network, or after getting advance approval — something impossible when someone is having a heart attack. This bill would have required group health plans and insurers to cover emergency services whenever a reasonable person would consider the situation an emergency, with no prior authorization, regardless of which hospital or doctor treated the patient. It also would have covered follow-up care after an ER visit and limited extra charges for using an out-of-network emergency room, and applied the same rules to Medicare and Medicaid managed-care plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with employer-sponsored or individual health insurance, including Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries enrolled in private plans. The biggest gainers are people who end up in an emergency room outside their plan's network — often because they were unconscious, taken by ambulance, or facing an urgent situation — and who would otherwise face surprise bills or outright denials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured patients facing surprise ER bills

how_it_helps.text: Plans would have to cover emergency services with no prior authorization determination required, so patients would not need approval before seeking emergency care [S3].

Coverage would apply whether or not the treating hospital or physician is in the plan's network, whenever the patient could not reach a network hospital, a reasonable layperson would expect harm from delay, or a plan doctor referred them there [S3].

The bill defines an emergency by the 'prudent layperson' standard — what an average person would reasonably believe needs immediate care, including severe pain — instead of leaving the final diagnosis to the insurer [S3].

Plans would have to cover medically necessary maintenance and post-stabilization care at out-of-network hospitals once the treating physician sought authorization, with strict timelines forcing the plan to respond or lose the ability to deny [S3].

Extra cost-sharing for using a nonparticipating provider would be barred in the exceptional cases, and kept to a reasonable differential in others, and plans would have to educate members on how to use emergency services and 911 [S3].
The same protections would extend to Medicare managed care, Medicaid private plans, and Medicare Select policies, with states barred from waiving the Medicaid requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and the employers that sponsor them would bear the added cost of paying for out-of-network emergency and follow-up care, limiting a cost-control tool managed-care plans used to steer patients to network hospitals. Some of that cost could show up in premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate would raise plan costs — paying out-of-network emergency rates and limiting cost-sharing differentials removes a tool plans used to keep premiums down, and some of the cost would likely be passed to all enrollees through higher premiums [S3].

The rules around post-stabilization care are highly technical — 30-minute response windows, good-faith contact requirements, and physician-to-physician call procedures — creating a layer of compliance complexity and disputes between treating physicians and plan reviewers [S3].

Critics of coverage mandates in this era argued that federal requirements reduce employer flexibility to design benefits and push smaller employers toward dropping coverage altogether; no such testimony is in the provided record, but this was the standard objection to benefit mandates of the period.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protection addresses a real and frightening failure of 1990s managed care: people got emergency treatment and then received denials or large surprise bills because the nearest ER was out of network. The cost is real but targeted — it applies only when the plan already covers emergency services, and it preserves network rules in ordinary cases. The bill's main design weakness is procedural complexity around follow-up care, not the underlying patient protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to three subcommittees, and none of them ever took it up — it sat there until the 105th Congress ended in January 1999 without a single vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ben Cardin introduced the bill on February 25, 1997, with 26 original cosponsors from both parties, including Republicans Marge Roukema, Christopher Shays, and Charlie Norwood [S3].
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Commerce, and Education and the Workforce Committees on the day it was introduced [S5].

In March 1997 it was referred to the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, the Education and the Workforce Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, and the Commerce Health and Environment Subcommittee — the last recorded action on the bill [S5].
No committee or subcommittee ever reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1].
By the end it had gathered 242 cosponsors — 81 Republicans, 160 Democrats, and 1 Independent — well over half the House [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed-care plans that kept their discretion to deny or heavily charge for out-of-network emergency care, and employers who avoided any increase in health benefit costs. Insured patients gained nothing until the idea was enacted through later legislation.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was strongly bipartisan — 81 Republicans and 160 Democrats signed on — and the bill's original cosponsors included Republicans from both moderate and conservative wings, so this was not a party-line fight; the blocking happened quietly in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have forced plans to pay for out-of-network emergency and follow-up care and capped how much extra cost-sharing they could charge, removing both a claims-denial practice and a network-steering tool. Their gain from the bill dying was continued ability to deny or surcharge emergency care, at insured patients' expense. [S3]
Employers would bear the added cost of broader emergency coverage, possibly through higher premiums. Their interest in lower costs pulled against employees' interest in covered emergency care. [S3]
Hospitals and emergency doctors, especially those outside plan networks, would be paid for care they were often left to write off or chase in disputes with plans. [S3]
